description: We are two students in Singapore working on AI and software. We built TRIX, an AI medical crew member for astronauts far from Earth. It does two-minute daily health checks against each astronaut’s own normal, uses 13 AI agents with NASA-sourced answers, shows a 3D guide in emergencies, and works offline when the link to Earth is cut. Our skills: AI/ML, multi-agent systems, full-stack web, data and UX design.
summary:
When Earth is 20 minutes away, who checks on the astronaut? From Mars, help takes up to 40 minutes, so a missed warning sign can become an emergency before Earth knows. We built TRIX: health monitoring software that acts as an AI medical crew member on board, from launch to landing, even with the Earth link cut.

Reinforcement learning learns when each astronaut responds and prompts a two-minute check. Astronauts talk to TRIX: speech is transcribed into readings, with steps read aloud in 10 languages. Voice biomarkers and computer vision detect fatigue and guide ECG placement and CPR. Multi-agent orchestration in LangGraph (13 agents in 3 teams) compares each astronaut with their own normal (CUSUM, Isolation Forest), explains results with RAG-cited NASA sources, and shows every decision in an agent tree.

In an emergency, a 3D guide acts out procedures like zero-gravity CPR while every crew tablet raises the alarm. A weekly body scan and landing-readiness score track the body.

Gamification keeps the habit: checks earn streaks, badges and a crew goal (never for good numbers), and recorded messages from family unlock as rewards, with one played at once on a hard day.

Using NASA OSDR and 374 ISS experiments, TRIX caught 8 of 8 problems in a simulated 240-day mission, flagging bone loss 35 days earlier than fixed limits.
details:
What TRIX does

On long-duration missions, a reply from Earth can take up to 40 minutes, so astronauts must be able to detect and respond to health problems on their own. TRIX (Triage, Response & Intelligence eXpert) is an onboard AI medical crew member built for this situation. It runs on the spacecraft’s own computer, keeps working when the link to Earth is cut, and supports each astronaut from launch to landing.

Each day, TRIX guides the astronaut through a two-minute check of the six vitals named in the NASA brief, along with fatigue, vision, symptoms and nutrition. Every result is explained in plain language and given a GO, WATCH or NO-GO status with one clear next step. In an emergency, a realistic 3D crew member demonstrates the procedure step by step, with 360° rotation, zoom and slow motion, while an alert is raised on every crew tablet. Each week, a camera body scan outlines the astronaut and compares today’s shape with day 1. It measures the changes spaceflight causes, such as a puffier face from fluid shift and thinner calves from muscle loss, and recommends exercise to address them. Before landing, TRIX scores readiness for gravity and produces a recovery plan. Reports to Earth respect each astronaut’s privacy settings and are sent with the real communication delay.

Guided medical procedures

Most crew members rarely practise emergency medicine, so TRIX guides them through eight procedures: ECG recording, CPR in microgravity, blood glucose testing, low-oxygen response, radiation shelter, post-spacewalk checks, cardiac ultrasound and the landing stand test. When the Emergency team identifies a problem, it selects the right procedure and starts it immediately. Each procedure moves forward one step at a time and is read aloud, and the crew member can control it by voice while their hands are busy. A realistic 3D crew member demonstrates each step, and the camera checks the work as it happens. It tells the user how many centimetres to move an ECG sticker, counts CPR compressions against the target of 110 per minute, and checks ultrasound image quality. The steps are locked to the approved protocol, so the AI can explain a step but can never add, skip or reorder one. A practice mode scores rehearsals, so the crew can train before they ever need it.

How it works

TRIX is built on multi-agent orchestration using LangGraph, organised in two levels. A mission orchestrator classifies each event and routes it to one of three team orchestrators: Daily Care, Emergency and Operations, which together coordinate 13 specialised agents. When Daily Care detects a critical reading, it hands the case to Emergency automatically. A shared Safety agent reviews every response and blocks unsafe advice, such as unapproved medicines, doses or diagnoses. Every step is recorded in an agent tree, so the crew and flight surgeons can see exactly which agent acted and why.

Answers are grounded through retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). A hybrid BM25 and TF-IDF search retrieves NASA Human Research Program material, NASA-STD-3001 limits and onboard procedures, and every answer cites its source; when no source applies, TRIX says so rather than guessing. Detection uses machine learning that is personal to each astronaut: robust baselines, CUSUM to catch slow drift, and an Isolation Forest with SHAP to explain unusual combinations of signals. A reinforcement-learning bandit (Thompson sampling) learns when each astronaut actually responds and schedules check-ins at that time, which raised response rates from 54% to 72%.

TRIX is designed to be used hands-free. Speech is transcribed into readings and commands, so an astronaut can say “118 over 76” or “start CPR” without touching the screen, and voice biomarkers flag fatigue from changes in pace, pauses and pitch. Each astronaut chooses one of 10 languages, including English, Russian, Japanese, Chinese, French, Spanish and Hindi. TRIX then listens in that language: an astronaut can speak naturally in their own language, and their words are transcribed and understood as readings or commands. The interface, instructions and spoken guidance follow the same choice, so international crews can follow instructions under pressure in their own language. Computer vision with MediaPipe and OpenCV measures eye closure, guides ECG placement and counts CPR rate, all on the device. Language generation uses Claude through the Anthropic API, with a local Llama 3.2 model as an offline fallback.

Beyond the daily routine

TRIX adapts to where the crew is. Its advice changes for a space station, Moon base, Moon rover or Mars spacecraft, for example when weightlessness rules out a scale or no ground crew will be waiting at landing. It watches the environment as well as the body. It follows live NASA DONKI solar storm data and moves the crew to the shelter procedure when a storm arrives, and it links cabin CO₂ levels to reported headaches. Crew care extends to a daily buddy check, medicine stock forecasts, a food pouch scan for nutrition and skin photo tracking. Everything comes together on a single Mission Deck. For evaluation and training, a what-if simulator runs seven emergencies through the real agents, a “cut the link” mode shows TRIX deciding on board with no contact with Earth, a mission replay covers 240 simulated days, and a flight surgeon view shows exactly what reaches Earth. All 57 features are described in FEATURES.md.

Why it is better, and its impact

Most health monitoring relies on fixed limits and assumes a doctor is close at hand. TRIX compares each astronaut with their own normal, so it catches gradual changes that fixed limits miss. In a simulated 240-day, three-astronaut mission, it detected all eight planted health events, compared with seven for fixed limits. It flagged accelerated bone loss 35 days earlier and rising blood pressure 25 days earlier, and blocked 20 of 20 unsafe responses. Rather than only displaying numbers, it explains them, demonstrates what to do, and makes its reasoning transparent.

TRIX also addresses the human side of long missions. Gamification through streaks, badges and a shared crew goal rewards completing checks, never good results, so astronauts have no reason to hide a bad reading. Recorded messages from family and friends unlock as rewards, and on a difficult day one is released at once, helping counter isolation, one of NASA’s five spaceflight hazards. The same approach could support people in remote settings on Earth, such as polar stations, ships and rural clinics.

Tools and considerations

TRIX is built with Python (FastAPI, SQLite, LangGraph, scikit-learn, OpenCV) and JavaScript (three.js, MediaPipe, Web Speech). It draws on NASA OSDR Inspiration4 studies, the ISS Research Explorer, NASA HRP, NASA-STD-3001 and NASA DONKI. Claude assisted with development under the team’s direction, and the system is verified by 392 automated tests. The design was guided by communication delay, offline operation, safety, privacy and long-term motivation. Crew data is simulated, and the next step is validation with real devices in an analog mission.
